mcqs.question: A checkbox has visible text "Subscribe to newsletter" right next to it. Which labeling approach is preferred, and why?
options: aria-label="Subscribe to newsletter", since it's the most explicit way to set an accessible name
aria-labelledby pointing at a separate hidden span containing the same text
No labeling is needed since the text is already visible on screen
A real <label for> (or wrapping <label>) linked to the checkbox, since it both provides the accessible name and expands the clickable target to include the label text
mcqs.explanation: A real <label> is preferred whenever visible text already exists — it does everything aria-label does for accessible naming while also expanding the actual clickable/tappable hit area to the whole label, a real usability win aria-label alone doesn't provide. Visible text with no programmatic association still gives assistive tech nothing, so "no labeling needed" is incorrect, and duplicating the same text in a hidden aria-labelledby target adds unnecessary indirection for no benefit here.

mcqs.question: An input has a visible red error message right below it in the DOM, but no aria-describedby. What does a screen reader announce when the field receives focus?
options: The field's label and type only — the error text is not announced unless explicitly associated via aria-describedby
The label, type, and error text together, since visual proximity implies the association automatically
Only the error text, skipping the field's label entirely
An error tone/beep, with no textual announcement
mcqs.explanation: Visual proximity in the DOM conveys nothing to a screen reader on its own — aria-describedby is the explicit, required mechanism that links the two, so without it only the field's own label and type get announced and the error text is silently skipped. There's no automatic error tone triggered by unassociated text, and the error text is never announced without the label being announced too.

mcqs.question: A form-wide error summary appears after a failed submission while focus is still on the submit button. Which mechanism announces the new summary text to a screen reader without moving the user's focus away from where they currently are?
options: aria-hidden="false" on the summary element
A tabindex="0" attribute added to the summary
aria-live="polite" on the summary region, announcing the change once it appears
role="heading" on the summary element
mcqs.explanation: aria-live="polite" is specifically designed to announce content changes without stealing focus from wherever the user currently is, which is exactly the requirement here. tabindex and role="heading" don't trigger an announcement of a content change on their own, and aria-hidden="false" is simply the (often already-default) non-hidden state, not a live-announcement mechanism.

mcqs.question: An error summary at the top of a form is wired with `role="alert"`, `aria-live="assertive"`, and an explicit `.focus()` call on submission failure. Why use assertive instead of polite here, given assertive is generally discouraged for routine feedback?
options: Assertive is always the safer default and should be used for all live regions
A failed form submission is exactly the urgent, blocking case assertive is designed for, unlike routine feedback such as a save confirmation
Polite would prevent the .focus() call from working at all
Assertive and polite behave identically in practice, so the choice doesn't matter
mcqs.explanation: Assertive is reserved for genuinely urgent interruptions, and a blocked form submission is a legitimate case for it — the general guidance to prefer polite applies to routine feedback, not this scenario. Polite wouldn't interfere with a .focus() call, which is a separate mechanism from the live-region announcement, and the two live-region types are not interchangeable or equivalent.

mcqs.question: A form indicates invalid fields with only a red border, no text or icon. Besides screen reader users, who else is affected by this?
options: Color-blind users, for whom a red border may be indistinguishable from a normal one, and anyone viewing the page under degraded color conditions like bright sunlight or grayscale mode
Only users with a specific browser extension installed
No one else — this only affects screen reader users
Only users on older browser versions that don't support CSS border-color
mcqs.explanation: Color-only indication fails multiple real, distinct groups at once — color-blind users, and anyone in a context where color rendering is degraded — not just screen reader users, which is why WCAG's Use of Color criterion requires a non-color signal in addition. This is unrelated to any specific browser extension or CSS border-color support, both of which are broadly supported.

mcqs.question: A required field is marked with a visible asterisk but has neither the native `required` attribute nor `aria-required="true"`. What's missing for a screen reader user?
options: There's no gap — the asterisk alone is sufficient for all users
The field will fail to submit regardless of what the user enters
The screen reader has no way to announce that the field is required, since the asterisk is a purely visual marker with no programmatic equivalent
The field becomes unfocusable entirely without one of these attributes
mcqs.explanation: A visual asterisk carries no information to a screen reader unless the field is also marked required (announced natively) or aria-required="true" — without either, a screen reader user has no way to know the field is mandatory before attempting to submit. The field remains focusable and submittable either way; the gap is purely about whether the requirement is communicated, not whether the form functions.
